title: Robot Motion Planning
notes: Open by grounding the lecture in the assigned chapter span, printed pages 283-306, while noting that the manifest also records PDF pages 294-317. The chapter is a sequence of reductions: a robot placement becomes a point, collision becomes membership in forbidden configuration space, and continuous feasibility becomes graph reachability in a roadmap.

title: Modeling Contract
notes: Use this slide to separate robotics reality from the chapter model. The real application has sensing, dynamics, uncertainty, and actuators. The computational geometry model deliberately freezes the world into known polygonal obstacles and a polygonal robot so that collision-free motion can be studied as an exact planar geometric problem.

title: Configurations Are Points
notes: Define the key abstraction slowly. The work-space robot may occupy a two-dimensional region, but a placement is encoded by a small parameter vector. A translating planar robot has two degrees of freedom, while allowing rotation adds the angle parameter and changes the topology because zero and one full turn are identified.

title: Free, Forbidden, C-Obstacles
notes: Make the collision predicate the star of the slide. A configuration is forbidden exactly when the placed robot intersects an obstacle; the C-obstacle is the set of all such parameter points for one obstacle. Mention the convention used here: touching is treated as forbidden, so the planned route stays in the open free region.

title: Point Robot Free Space
notes: Now reduce to the first algorithmic case. For a point robot, work space and configuration space coincide, so the forbidden region is just the polygonal obstacles. The trapezoidal map from Chapter 6 decomposes the remaining free area by vertical extensions, giving the finite cells that later carry the roadmap nodes.

title: Roadmap Query
notes: Explain the roadmap path as three geometric pieces. First connect the start point to the center node of its trapezoid, then traverse graph edges through wall nodes and cell centers, and finally connect the goal cell center to the goal. Point location supplies the start and goal cells before the graph search begins.

title: Roadmap Completeness Proof
notes: Give the correctness proof as a deformation argument rather than a formal wall of text. Any continuous free path crosses a sequence of trapezoids. Consecutive trapezoids share a vertical wall segment, and the roadmap includes a node on that wall, so the cell sequence can be converted into a graph path without leaving free space.

title: C-Obstacle Equals Minkowski Sum
notes: This is the central reduction for a translating polygonal robot. If a placed robot intersects an obstacle, some robot point and obstacle point coincide, which means the reference point lies in the obstacle plus the reflected robot. Conversely, any point in that Minkowski sum gives a contact witness, so the inflated obstacle is exactly the forbidden set.

title: Convex Minkowski Algorithm
notes: Focus on the edge-angle walk. For convex polygons, the boundary of the sum is obtained by merging the directed edge sequences by polar angle. The support direction viewpoint explains why no more than n plus m edges appear: every output edge advances at least one input edge sequence.

title: Pseudodiscs
notes: Introduce pseudodiscs as the union-complexity hinge. Inflated convex obstacles generated from disjoint convex pieces behave as shapes whose boundaries meet at most twice. The useful intuition is directional: for a fixed direction, the supporting features line up over connected intervals, preventing repeated alternation on the union boundary.

title: Union Complexity Proof Move
notes: Make the charging argument inspectable. Boundary crossings that survive on the union can be charged to original vertices and pseudodisc intersections rather than to all pairwise overlays. The punchline for the lecture is that the union is linear in total input complexity, which keeps the later translational planner from exploding quadratically.

title: Translational Planning Pipeline
notes: Assemble the algorithmic pipeline after the geometry work. Triangulate the obstacles, build one C-obstacle for each triangle by Minkowski inflation, compute the union of forbidden space, decompose the remaining free space, and query the roadmap. State the preprocessing bound O(n log squared n) and the linear query bound for the reported path.

title: Rotation Adds A Cylinder
notes: Now add the third parameter. The configuration space for a planar robot that both translates and rotates is R squared times a circle, not ordinary three-space. Horizontal slices at fixed orientation are ordinary translational problems, but as the orientation changes the C-obstacle cross-section twists through configuration space.

title: Slice Roadmaps And Failures
notes: Use the two-slice picture to explain both the method and its weakness. Within one slice, translational paths are checked exactly. The risky step is connecting nearby slices: both endpoint placements may be collision-free, while an intermediate orientation along the rotation arc collides with an obstacle.

title: Enlarged Robot And Alternatives
notes: Discuss the sweep enlargement as a conservative repair. If the robot is replaced by a shape containing the region swept during a half-step of rotation, then accepted inter-slice rotations of the original robot are safer. The cost is false negatives, so the slide also names exact cell decompositions, retraction roadmaps, potential fields, and probabilistic roadmaps as alternative planning philosophies.
